hero.headline: Gulliver at 300, Seen Through a 1933 Pulp Story Set in the Year 3000
hero.dek: Tom Dillon, writing on the University of Liverpool's special collections blog, marks the 300th anniversary of Gulliver's Travels, first published on 28 October 1726, by turning to science fiction. Leslie F. Stone's "Gulliver, 3000 A.D.", printed in Wonder Stories in May 1933 with illustrations by Frank R. Paul, strands a space captain on Mars, where he is enslaved by six-inch green aliens and fights their enemies, six-inch copper aliens he names Lilliputians. Dillon reads the story as a critique of racism, notes that Swift both criticised colonialism and invested in the South Sea Company, and launches the library's digital exhibition Gulliver's Travels: Before and Beyond.
hero.byline: By Tom Dillon · Manuscripts and More

hero.dek: Ross, writing on the National Records of Scotland blog, presents a plan of the order of the Battle of Culloden, fought on 16 April 1746, as the third in a series on striking and interesting items the archive holds. The plan marks the point at which the Royal army wheeled into order of battle, just south of Castle Stuart, turning towards Castle Dalcross. The battle set the King's army under William Augustus, Duke of Cumberland, against the Jacobite army under Charles Edward Stuart and lasted under an hour. About 1,250 Jacobites were killed, while the government force officially lost 50 men, with 259 wounded. The text comes from the archive's 2025 book Treasures of National Records of Scotland.

Gray owns the entire 27-image Incidents set from 2012, which Wessel called fictional analogies, leaving the viewer to make sense of the possibilities. Glass cases intermingle prints with magazines, books and maquettes. With no comprehensive institutional retrospective since Wessel died in 2018, Knoblauch finds the show expands beyond his early California work to Richmond houses, Los Angeles at night and Las Vegas.

hero.dek: William Fawcett visits Church Rate Corner, a late masterpiece by the Arts-and-Crafts architect M. H. Baillie Scott, set in central Cambridge with no street frontage. Designed in 1924 for Marjorie Duckett as her married home with Arthur Sewell, who died in 1926, it later housed Joan and Stanley Bennett for more than 50 years and now belongs to Michael Nedo and Gillian Moore, only its third owners. Photographed by Will Pryce, the piece walks the almost symmetrical garden front, the south-facing rooms, the plain timber stair and oak-board doors, and a gravity-fed heating system still in operation. Diane Haigh, the author's late wife, was conservation architect for its 1992 restoration.

hero.headline: An Organist Plays and Ranks All 606 Hymns in the New English Hymnal
hero.dek: Maddie Lay, an Oxford-based arts writer and part-time church organist, spent a month playing through all 606 entries in the New English Hymnal and ranked every one. Its ancestor, the English Hymnal of 1906, was compiled by Percy Dearmer and Ralph Vaughan Williams, and was initially banned by the Archbishop of Canterbury, lest it dethrone the popular Hymns Ancient and Modern. The 1986 revision kept roughly two-thirds of the original numbers and added about a hundred more. Lay ranks them from the depths of hell to the heights of heaven, as a guide to which hymns deepen worship and which can be safely ignored.

hero.dek: Lisa Cain looks at Estudio CRU's identity for Mirá, a São Paulo bakery that joins Japanese and Brazilian baking. She grounds it in Brazil's Japanese diaspora, more than two million people and the largest outside Japan, whose families adapted home methods to local ingredients, pickling papaya, watermelon and chayote. The identity sets Nikkei Maru, a typeface inspired by the lettering on immigrant-run shops, restaurants and hotels, against oversized Latin type and earthy colours. Cain's argument is that fusion branding usually lines up two countries' symbols, where this one shows how the traditions actually came together.

Montagu James itemises what went, the Act I and III ballets, the Act II hunters' chorus, the Mathilde and Arnold duet, and notes these cuts were milder than most. He is specific about the singing, with Konu Kim's effortless Asile hereditaire the standout and George Gagnidze's Tell a mixed evening of muffled diction redeemed by one convincing Sois immobile, and he is unpersuaded by the dystopian staging's Alpine postcard projections and CGI storm. The argument underneath is about programming: that a regional company builds an audience faster on an ambitious neglected work than on another run at the canon.
